CloudFront metrics like Requests, error rates, and bytes transferred live in us-east-1 regardless of distribution region, so I'll need to query there. Run the EKS 'ui' workload with >1 replica spread across Availability Zones so a single pod is no longer a single point of failure.**\n\nThe target group k8s-ui-ui-0000000005 had exactly one registered target (pod IP 10.0.0.10:8080, us-west-2b). Set the 'ui' Deployment replicas to >=2 (preferably 3), add topologySpreadConstraints/podAntiAffinity across topology.kubernetes.io/zone, and a PodDisruptionBudget (minAvailable>=1). NLB cross-zone LB is already enabled, so extra replicas receive traffic immediately.\n\nAcceptance criteria:\n- The 'ui' Deployment (namespace ui, cluster example-shop) has replicas>=2 with pods in >=2 AZs\n- describe-target-health on k8s-ui-ui-0000000005 shows >=2 healthy targets in distinct AZs\n- A PodDisruptionBudget guarantees >=1 pod stays available during voluntary disruptions\n\n**2. Add HTTP readiness/liveness probes and resource requests/limits to the EKS 'ui' workload so the orchestrator detects and self-heals the application-layer failure mode seen here.**\n\nThe incident was an app-layer failure where TCP was accepted but no HTTP was served, invisible to TCP health checks. Add an httpGet readiness probe (remove a non-serving pod from the NLB target group) and an httpGet liveness probe (restart a hung pod) on port 8080, plus CPU/memory requests and limits to bound an OOM/resource driver.\n\nAcceptance criteria:\n- The 'ui' container defines httpGet readiness and liveness probes on port 8080 against a path that returns 200 only when it can serve\n- The 'ui' container defines CPU and memory requests and limits\n- A pod that accepts TCP but fails HTTP is removed from the target group and/or restarted\n\n**3. Codify the NLB target group HTTP health check in the Kubernetes Service manifest so the manual change does not drift.**\n\nIf the target group is reconciled by the AWS Load Balancer Controller, the manual HTTP health-check change reverts on reconcile. Set service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-protocol: HTTP, -healthcheck-path, -healthcheck-port on the 'ui' Service.\n\nAcceptance criteria:\n- The 'ui' Service manifest declares the HTTP health-check protocol, path, and port annotations\n- After an AWS Load Balancer Controller reconcile, k8s-ui-ui-0000000005 retains HealthCheckProtocol HTTP\n\n**4. Codify the CloudFront origin failover, corrected origin DNS, and S3 fallback in Terraform so the resilience config is durable and reproducible.**\n\nThe distribution is Terraform-managed. Represent the primary origin via a stable reference to the live NLB (so it tracks NLB recreation rather than hardcoding a generated DNS that goes stale), the S3 fallback bucket + OAC + least-privilege policy, and the origin_group with failover codes 500/502/503/504.\n\nAcceptance criteria:\n- terraform plan shows no drift after the manual changes are applied\n- The CloudFront primary origin is derived from a stable reference to the live NLB, not a hardcoded generated DNS that breaks on recreation\n- The origin group and S3 fallback bucket/OAC/policy are fully declared in Terraform","children":[]}]}]}]}}

**1. Run the EKS 'ui' workload with >1 replica spread across Availability Zones so a single pod is no longer a single point of failure.**

The target group k8s-ui-ui-0000000005 had exactly one registered target (pod IP 10.0.0.10:8080, us-west-2b). Set the 'ui' Deployment replicas to >=2 (preferably 3), add topologySpreadConstraints/podAntiAffinity across topology.kubernetes.io/zone, and a PodDisruptionBudget (minAvailable>=1). NLB cross-zone LB is already enabled, so extra replicas receive traffic immediately.

Acceptance criteria:
- The 'ui' Deployment (namespace ui, cluster example-shop) has replicas>=2 with pods in >=2 AZs
- describe-target-health on k8s-ui-ui-0000000005 shows >=2 healthy targets in distinct AZs
- A PodDisruptionBudget guarantees >=1 pod stays available during voluntary disruptions

**2. Add HTTP readiness/liveness probes and resource requests/limits to the EKS 'ui' workload so the orchestrator detects and self-heals the application-layer failure mode seen here.**

The incident was an app-layer failure where TCP was accepted but no HTTP was served, invisible to TCP health checks. Add an httpGet readiness probe (remove a non-serving pod from the NLB target group) and an httpGet liveness probe (restart a hung pod) on port 8080, plus CPU/memory requests and limits to bound an OOM/resource driver.

Acceptance criteria:
- The 'ui' container defines httpGet readiness and liveness probes on port 8080 against a path that returns 200 only when it can serve
- The 'ui' container defines CPU and memory requests and limits
- A pod that accepts TCP but fails HTTP is removed from the target group and/or restarted

**3. Codify the NLB target group HTTP health check in the Kubernetes Service manifest so the manual change does not drift.**

If the target group is reconciled by the AWS Load Balancer Controller, the manual HTTP health-check change reverts on reconcile. Set service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-protocol: HTTP, -healthcheck-path, -healthcheck-port on the 'ui' Service.

Acceptance criteria:
- The 'ui' Service manifest declares the HTTP health-check protocol, path, and port annotations
- After an AWS Load Balancer Controller reconcile, k8s-ui-ui-0000000005 retains HealthCheckProtocol HTTP

**4. Codify the CloudFront origin failover, corrected origin DNS, and S3 fallback in Terraform so the resilience config is durable and reproducible.**

The distribution is Terraform-managed. Represent the primary origin via a stable reference to the live NLB (so it tracks NLB recreation rather than hardcoding a generated DNS that goes stale), the S3 fallback bucket + OAC + least-privilege policy, and the origin_group with failover codes 500/502/503/504.

Acceptance criteria:
- terraform plan shows no drift after the manual changes are applied
- The CloudFront primary origin is derived from a stable reference to the live NLB, not a hardcoded generated DNS that breaks on recreation
- The origin group and S3 fallback bucket/OAC/policy are fully declared in Terraform","children":[]}]}]}]}}

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### Timeouts & connection failures on example-shop UI (EEXAMPLE000001)
**Description:** On the only CloudFront distribution serving traffic (EEXAMPLE000001, example-shop UI, EKS origin in us-west-2), request volume collapsed ~86–91% starting at 16:05 — from ~11,000 per 5-min to a trough of 963 at 16:15 — recovering by 16:25. The collapse in completed request volume (rather than a surge of edge-returned status codes) matches user-reported timeouts and connection failures.
**Time:** 2026-10-11T16:05:00Z - 2026-10-11T16:25:00Z

## Findings

### Cause: EKS origin (us-west-2) availability failure behind EEXAMPLE000001
**Description:** The impaired distribution's traffic collapsed ~86–91% with an exclusively 5xx error signal and no 4xx — consistent with the EKS origin in us-west-2 becoming unreachable or overloaded ~16:05–16:25. Pending confirmation from EKS/ALB origin health.
**Cascades to:** symptom-timeouts

#### Gaps
- **EKS 'ui' application-layer trigger not directly confirmed:** The deepest driver of the origin app-layer failure (pod crashloop/OOM/readiness failure/application error behind 10.0.0.10:8080, namespace ui, us-west-2, 16:05–16:25 UTC) could not be inspected: kubectl access to cluster example-shop was unavailable and the incident-era pod/NLB have since been replaced. CloudTrail for the ELB create/delete timeline was permission-blocked in the confirming session. This is the handoff lead for the next origin-investigation phase.
- **Incident-era origin infrastructure since replaced:** The NLB serving EEXAMPLE000001 during the incident (hash 235939453c7ba3a0) was deleted and recreated (current hash deed3f1375016a93, created 2026-10-15 04:01:58 UTC; an intermediate generation ad9260b20663ce89 also exists). Incident-window metrics were still recoverable via the retained historical LB dimension, but the live resources cannot be inspected for the incident state.

### Hypothesis: WebACL CreatedByCloudFront-a1b2c3d4 AntiDDoS rule may be blocking/challenging legitimate traffic
**Description:** The WebACL on the example-shop UI distribution (EEXAMPLE000001) was last modified 2026-10-06, ~5 days before the incident. Its priority-0 rule is AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet with client-side Challenge UsageOfAction=ENABLED, Sensitivity=HIGH, and SensitivityToBlock=LOW. An aggressive challenge/low block threshold could manifest as viewer timeouts/connection failures rather than clean 403s, matching the reported symptom. Still unconfirmed pending WAF metrics and CloudTrail change correlation.
**Cascades to:** symptom-timeouts

#### Gaps
- **EKS 'ui' application-layer trigger not directly confirmed:** The deepest driver of the origin app-layer failure (pod crashloop/OOM/readiness failure/application error behind 10.0.0.10:8080, namespace ui, us-west-2, 16:05–16:25 UTC) could not be inspected: kubectl access to cluster example-shop was unavailable and the incident-era pod/NLB have since been replaced. CloudTrail for the ELB create/delete timeline was permission-blocked in the confirming session. This is the handoff lead for the next origin-investigation phase.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Harden the CloudFront → EKS origin path against single-origin failure: (1) correct the distribution's stale origin DNS to the live NLB; (2) add a CloudFront origin group with an S3 static-fallback secondary origin so an origin outage returns a maintenance page instead of total client-facing timeouts; (3) switch the NLB target group health check from TCP to HTTP so an application-layer failure is actually detected. Durable fixes (replicas>1 across AZs, probes, resource limits, and codifying everything in IaC) are captured as a code change specification.

## Reasoning
The 2026-10-11 incident self-recovered and had no triggering change to roll back; root cause is an application-layer failure of the single EKS 'ui' workload behind the distribution's only origin. Current-state inspection confirmed three vulnerabilities that make this failure total rather than partial: stale origin DNS (points at deleted NLB 235939453c7ba3a0), single origin with no failover, and a TCP-only health check on a single-target NLB that cannot see app-layer death. None of these touch AWS WAF or the WebACL association. EKS-side changes could not be applied because kubectl access to cluster example-shop was unavailable, so they are delivered as a code change specification.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Pre Validate

#### 1.1 Confirm the live NLB and its DNS name so the corrected origin points at…
**Type:** command
```
aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --region us-west-2 --load-balancer-arns [redacted ARN] --query 'LoadBalancers[0].{DNSName:DNSName,State:State.Code}'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the live NLB and its DNS name so the corrected origin points at a resolvable, active endpoint.

#### 1.2 Verify current target health and replica count — confirm whether only…
**Type:** command
```
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --region us-west-2 --target-group-arn [redacted ARN]
```
**Purpose:** Verify current target health and replica count — confirm whether only the single pod IP 10.0.0.10:8080 is registered (the SPOF the plan addresses).

### Step 2: Prepare

#### 2.1 Back up the current distribution config and ETag so the exact prior…
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudfront get-distribution-config --region us-east-1 --id EEXAMPLE000001 > example-shop-dist-backup.json
```
**Purpose:** Back up the current distribution config and ETag so the exact prior state can be restored on rollback.
**Risks:** Record the ETag; it is the IfMatch value for the apply update and the baseline for rollback.

#### 2.2 Back up the current TCP health-check config so it can be restored on…
**Type:** command
```
aws elbv2 describe-target-groups --region us-west-2 --target-group-arns [redacted ARN] > example-shop-tg-backup.json
```
**Purpose:** Back up the current TCP health-check config so it can be restored on rollback.

#### 2.3 Create a private S3 bucket to host the static fallback/maintenance page…
**Type:** command
```
aws s3api create-bucket --region us-east-1 --bucket example-shop-ui-fallback-012345678901_1
```
**Purpose:** Create a private S3 bucket to host the static fallback/maintenance page (reached only via CloudFront OAC; keep Block Public Access on).

#### 2.4 Upload the static maintenance page CloudFront serves from the fallback…
**Type:** command
```
aws s3api put-object --region us-east-1 --bucket example-shop-ui-fallback-012345678901_1 --key index.html --content-type text/html --body maintenance.html
```
**Purpose:** Upload the static maintenance page CloudFront serves from the fallback origin on failover.

#### 2.5 Create an OAC so CloudFront can read the private fallback bucket…
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudfront create-origin-access-control --region us-east-1 --origin-access-control-config Name=example-shop-ui-fallback-oac,OriginAccessControlOriginType=s3,SigningBehavior=always,SigningProtocol=sigv4
```
**Purpose:** Create an OAC so CloudFront can read the private fallback bucket without making it public; record the returned OAC Id.

#### 2.6 Grant only this distribution read access to the fallback bucket, scoped…
**Type:** command
```
aws s3api put-bucket-policy --region us-east-1 --bucket example-shop-ui-fallback-012345678901_1 --policy '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Sid":"AllowCloudFrontServicePrincipalReadOnly","Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"cloudfront.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"[redacted ARN]","Condition":{"StringEquals":{"AWS:SourceArn":"[redacted ARN]"}}}]}'
```
**Purpose:** Grant only this distribution read access to the fallback bucket, scoped by SourceArn — no public or wildcard principals.

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 Correct the stale origin DNS to the live NLB and add origin failover…
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudfront update-distribution --region us-east-1 --id EEXAMPLE000001 --if-match <ETag-from-prepare-backup> --distribution-config file://example-shop-dist-updated.json
```
**Purpose:** Correct the stale origin DNS to the live NLB and add origin failover: update primary origin DomainName to k8s-ui-ui-0000000004.elb.us-west-2.amazonaws.com; add S3 fallback origin (ui-fallback-s3) with the OAC; add OriginGroup (members eks-ui-lb primary + ui-fallback-s3 secondary, FailoverCriteria 500,502,503,504); point DefaultCacheBehavior.TargetOriginId at the origin group; keep every other field identical to the backup.
**Risks:** Production entry point — a malformed DistributionConfig can disrupt delivery; modify only the five described fields., Failover triggers only on the configured 5xx codes; CloudFront maps origin unreachability/timeouts to 502/504, which are included, so this failure mode engages failover.

#### 3.2 Switch the NLB health check from TCP to HTTP so an app-layer failure…
**Type:** command
```
aws elbv2 modify-target-group --region us-west-2 --target-group-arn [redacted ARN] --health-check-protocol HTTP --health-check-port 8080 --health-check-path / --health-check-interval-seconds 10 --health-check-timeout-seconds 6 --healthy-threshold-count 3 --unhealthy-threshold-count 3
```
**Purpose:** Switch the NLB health check from TCP to HTTP so an app-layer failure (socket open, no payload) marks the target unhealthy — the exact detection gap behind this incident.
**Risks:** If the app does not return 200 on GET / , the HTTP check will mark the single target unhealthy and remove the origin; confirm the correct health-check path/code first and watch target health after applying.

### Step 4: Post Validate

#### 4.1 Confirm the change applied: OriginGroups=1, primary origin is the live…
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudfront get-distribution --region us-east-1 --id EEXAMPLE000001 --query 'Distribution.{Status:Status,OriginGroups:DistributionConfig.OriginGroups.Quantity,TargetOriginId:DistributionConfig.DefaultCacheBehavior.TargetOriginId,Origins:DistributionConfig.Origins.Items[].DomainName}'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the change applied: OriginGroups=1, primary origin is the live NLB DNS, secondary is the S3 fallback, TargetOriginId is the origin group, Status reaches Deployed.

#### 4.2 Confirm HealthCheckProtocol is now HTTP on path / 
**Type:** command
```
aws elbv2 describe-target-groups --region us-west-2 --target-group-arns [redacted ARN] --query 'TargetGroups[0].{Protocol:HealthCheckProtocol,Path:HealthCheckPath}'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm HealthCheckProtocol is now HTTP on path / .

#### 4.3 Confirm targets stay healthy under the new HTTP check and did not flap…
**Type:** command
```
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --region us-west-2 --target-group-arn [redacted ARN]
```
**Purpose:** Confirm targets stay healthy under the new HTTP check and did not flap; if any is unhealthy, fix the health-check path/code before considering the change complete.

### Step 5: Rollback

#### 5.1 Revert the distribution to its pre-change configuration if the origin…
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudfront update-distribution --region us-east-1 --id EEXAMPLE000001 --if-match <current-ETag-after-apply> --distribution-config file://example-shop-dist-backup-config-only.json
```
**Purpose:** Revert the distribution to its pre-change configuration if the origin group or corrected origin behaves unexpectedly.
**Risks:** Rollback restores the single-origin config including the stale origin DNS; prefer forward-fixing the primary origin DNS unless the new config is actively causing harm.

#### 5.2 Restore the original TCP health check if the HTTP check causes…
**Type:** command
```
aws elbv2 modify-target-group --region us-west-2 --target-group-arn [redacted ARN] --health-check-protocol TCP --health-check-port traffic-port --health-check-interval-seconds 10 --health-check-timeout-seconds 10 --healthy-threshold-count 3 --unhealthy-threshold-count 3
```
**Purpose:** Restore the original TCP health check if the HTTP check causes unexpected target flapping.
**Risks:** Reverting to TCP re-introduces the detection gap that masked this incident; prioritize fixing the health-check path instead.

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Run the EKS 'ui' workload with >1 replica spread across Availability Zones so a single pod is no longer a single point of failure.
**Description:** The target group k8s-ui-ui-0000000005 had exactly one registered target (pod IP 10.0.0.10:8080, us-west-2b). Set the 'ui' Deployment replicas to >=2 (preferably 3), add topologySpreadConstraints/podAntiAffinity across topology.kubernetes.io/zone, and a PodDisruptionBudget (minAvailable>=1). NLB cross-zone LB is already enabled, so extra replicas receive traffic immediately.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The 'ui' Deployment (namespace ui, cluster example-shop) has replicas>=2 with pods in >=2 AZs
- describe-target-health on k8s-ui-ui-0000000005 shows >=2 healthy targets in distinct AZs
- A PodDisruptionBudget guarantees >=1 pod stays available during voluntary disruptions

#### 2. Add HTTP readiness/liveness probes and resource requests/limits to the EKS 'ui' workload so the orchestrator detects and self-heals the application-layer failure mode seen here.
**Description:** The incident was an app-layer failure where TCP was accepted but no HTTP was served, invisible to TCP health checks. Add an httpGet readiness probe (remove a non-serving pod from the NLB target group) and an httpGet liveness probe (restart a hung pod) on port 8080, plus CPU/memory requests and limits to bound an OOM/resource driver.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The 'ui' container defines httpGet readiness and liveness probes on port 8080 against a path that returns 200 only when it can serve
- The 'ui' container defines CPU and memory requests and limits
- A pod that accepts TCP but fails HTTP is removed from the target group and/or restarted

#### 3. Codify the NLB target group HTTP health check in the Kubernetes Service manifest so the manual change does not drift.
**Description:** If the target group is reconciled by the AWS Load Balancer Controller, the manual HTTP health-check change reverts on reconcile. Set service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-protocol: HTTP, -healthcheck-path, -healthcheck-port on the 'ui' Service.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The 'ui' Service manifest declares the HTTP health-check protocol, path, and port annotations
- After an AWS Load Balancer Controller reconcile, k8s-ui-ui-0000000005 retains HealthCheckProtocol HTTP

#### 4. Codify the CloudFront origin failover, corrected origin DNS, and S3 fallback in Terraform so the resilience config is durable and reproducible.
**Description:** The distribution is Terraform-managed. Represent the primary origin via a stable reference to the live NLB (so it tracks NLB recreation rather than hardcoding a generated DNS that goes stale), the S3 fallback bucket + OAC + least-privilege policy, and the origin_group with failover codes 500/502/503/504.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- terraform plan shows no drift after the manual changes are applied
- The CloudFront primary origin is derived from a stable reference to the live NLB, not a hardcoded generated DNS that breaks on recreation
- The origin group and S3 fallback bucket/OAC/policy are fully declared in Terraform
